@graph.name: Local & Regional Move Operations
@graph.description: Local and regional move operations from survey to walkthrough. The operation chain runs survey, quote, pack, load, transport, unload, place, reassemble, unpack, and a final walkthrough. Survey runs through the quote form — Short (Quick Quote) default and Detailed Project, switching in place with the From, To and What's moving inputs preserved — or through the free film-only video walkthrough survey room, where the customer films and a person makes the estimate; nothing is auto-priced. The published scope is homes and businesses across the Shenandoah Valley and the Eastern Panhandle: packing and unpacking, loading and unloading, priced by the job, not by the hour, at one flat rate agreed in writing before move day. Load order runs heavy pieces low and first, room-staged boxes next, fragile items secured on top, everything strapped; placement is room by room by label, with reassembly of standard furniture. Transport follows the I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridors as the route fits. Both bases dispatch across the region — Winchester serves the Valley side, Martinsburg the Eastern Panhandle side, with overlap at Moorefield — and the quote form settles which crew and route fit the move. Where a move includes a high-mass piece of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, that item moves under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation with the KIM-GS Protocol and L/360 floor-deflection analysis, as part of the same flat-rate move. Home depth cross-references the residential category, business depth the office category, and moves beyond the region the long-distance category — cross-references are links, never duplicated claims.

@graph.name: Move Sizes & Access Operations
@graph.description: Move sizes and access operations for local and regional moves: the size bands, dwelling types, and access conditions that shape a local quote. Size bands, as demand shapes rather than company products: studio and one-bedroom homes, small jobs and partial loads, two-to-three-bedroom homes, four-plus-bedroom homes, and small offices. Dwelling and premises types: apartments, condos, townhomes, houses, estates, offices, and shops. Access conditions are quote inputs, never capability claims: stairs, elevator type and reservation, doorway and hallway width, parking and loading zones, long carry distance, building hours, and HOA rules. Staging runs through the driveway, yard, garage, or loading zone. Market reference data, labeled as such and never company times or prices: market guides plan studio and one-bedroom moves at roughly 3 to 5 hours with 2 movers, two-to-three-bedroom homes at 5 to 8 hours with 2 to 3 movers, and four-plus-bedroom homes at 8 to 12 hours with 3 to 4 movers; walk-up stairs, tight turns, elevator reservation windows, parking permits, and building move windows are the access factors that move a quote. The company publishes homes and businesses, with homeowners, renters, families, and seniors named on the branch pages, and no size-specific crew, equipment, minimum, or access capability is claimed anywhere in this dataset — the survey governs each job. Small-job depth continues as FAQ material on the existing pages, not a separate page, and apartment depth cross-references the residential category.

@graph.name: Commercial Terms & Cost Drivers
@graph.description: Commercial terms and cost drivers for local and regional moves. The company's only pricing term is the published one: a flat rate quoted in writing before move day, priced by the job, not by the hour — no hourly clock, ever — under the standing promise Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free! No company price, minimum, deposit, discount, fee, or surcharge is stated anywhere in this dataset. Every figure below is industry market data, researched and labeled as such, never a company term: local moves are priced by the hour in the market, typically a crew rate around $100 an hour for a two-person crew, often with two-to-four-hour minimums, plus travel and truck fees and extras; market totals in published guides run roughly $400 to $750 for a studio or one-bedroom home, $850 to $1,750 for two-to-three bedrooms, and $1,700 to $3,400 for four-plus bedrooms. The pricing models in the market: hourly (crew times hours, where the customer pays for every slow elevator, parking hunt, and delay), binding estimates (a fixed total for a listed scope and inventory), and flat-fee pricing (one guaranteed price set in advance from inventory, access, and distance). Under a flat or binding price the mover assumes the timing risk once the scope is locked; under hourly pricing the customer carries it. Cost drivers: inventory size, packing level, access — stairs, elevator, long carry — distance, and specialty items priced as separate line items. Booking windows in market guides: local moves book 2 to 4 weeks out off-peak and 4 to 8 weeks out in peak season, May through September with June busiest and month-ends and weekends tightest. The fear the flat rate answers is the hourly meter on a short local move; the company answer is one price in writing before the truck is loaded.

@graph.name: Buyer Personas & Trigger Events
@graph.description: Buyer personas and trigger events for local and regional moves. The personas: renters moving at a lease end, where apartment access and near-me search intent dominate; homeowners buying or selling inside the Shenandoah Valley and the Eastern Panhandle; families whose household is growing or shrinking; seniors relocating locally, cross-referenced to the senior category, which owns its claims; small-business owners changing premises, cross-referenced to the office and commercial categories; and closing-driven movers whose dates are set by a home purchase or sale. Trigger events: lease end, a home closing, a job transfer, household growth, household shrinkage, school-calendar timing, and a business premises change. Seasonality is industry research, labeled as such: peak season runs May through September, June is the most common moving month — one market dataset puts 41 percent of US moves in May through August — and month-end dates and weekends are the tightest; market guides put local booking windows at 2 to 4 weeks off-peak and 4 to 8 weeks in peak season. No availability promise is made anywhere in this dataset: the published branch hours are the hours, in every season. Search behavior from the company's own Search Console record: near-me intent is shared across the local and residential categories and converts fastest — 'movers near me' holds 246 impressions at position 5.0 with 11 clicks, the site's best click source — and Winchester-cluster searchers compare on price certainty and local presence. Every persona plans through the same quote path: the Short or Detailed quote form, or the film-only video walkthrough survey room with a human-made estimate.

@graph.name: Protection, Handling & Building Compliance
@graph.description: Protection, handling, and building compliance for local and regional moves. The published practice: loading and unloading with furniture protection on the path — blanket wrap and stretch wrap on the furniture, floor runners, and doorway and rail protection as the route requires; packing and unpacking as part of the service; disassembly and reassembly of standard furniture, planned up front; and, where a move includes a high-mass piece of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, SIR Structural Integrity Relocation under the KIM-GS Protocol with L/360 floor-deflection analysis. The survey room is film-only by rule: customers film their rooms and pieces, and never lift, move, open, or climb anything heavy or locked. Building conditions are planning inputs that shape the quote, never capability claims: elevator reservations and their windows, loading-zone reservations, building move hours, advance notice, HOA rules, and the certificate-of-insurance requirement that managed buildings commonly impose — an industry requirement, labeled as such. Industry reference, labeled as such: protection materials in the wider trade include boxes, dish barrels, wardrobe cartons, mattress bags, bubble wrap, stretch wrap, blankets, and labels, and standard market equipment includes dollies, ramps, and straps — an industry inventory, with no deployment claimed for the company. Liability education, labeled as such: valuation is not insurance, and the market's Full Value and Released Value ($0.60 per pound) options are explained in the commercial terms dataset as industry education only; no company coverage is claimed anywhere in this dataset. Heavy assets cross-reference the SIR heavy-asset category, custom crates the crating category, packing depth the packing category, and home-move protection depth the residential category.
